subject: Computer Networking
title: The Interface Message Processor
description: Learn The Interface Message Processor in one minute.

hook.text: ARPANET's computers were all different. A special machine sat between each one and the network — the IMP.

buildup.text: IMPs were refrigerator-sized routers. They handled packets so the host computers didn't have to.

discovery.text: BBN Technologies built the first IMPs in 1969. Each weighed about 900 pounds and cost hundreds of thousands.

twist.text: The IMP concept — separating networking from computing — is exactly how modern routers still work today.

climax.text: As ARPANET grew, IMPs were deployed at universities and labs. They became the physical backbone of the network.

punchline.text: IMPs were the first routers. Big, heavy, and revolutionary.

quiz.question: What was the role of an IMP in ARPANET?
options: It handled packet routing so host computers didn't have to
It stored all email messages for the network
It generated electricity for the network nodes

details.summary: The Interface Message Processor was a specialized computer that connected mainframes to ARPANET. Built by BBN Technologies, IMPs handled packet switching so that each university's existing computers did not need modification. They were the ancestors of modern routers.
details.whyItMatters: IMPs solved the critical problem of connecting different computers to a shared network without modifying each machine. This separation of networking from computing persists in every router today.
takeaways: IMPs were dedicated networking computers built by BBN
They isolated networking complexity from host computers
IMPs were the direct ancestors of modern routers

faq.question: Why were IMPs necessary for ARPANET?
faq.answer: Each university had a different mainframe with different software. Rather than modifying every computer to speak the network protocol, IMPs handled all networking. Host computers connected to their local IMP, and IMPs managed packet routing between sites.

faq.question: How are IMPs related to modern routers?
faq.answer: IMPs performed the same function as modern routers: receiving packets, determining the best path, and forwarding them. They maintained routing tables and handled error recovery. Modern routers are vastly faster and smaller but implement the same conceptual architecture.
